## Current Code Workflow (from code analyzer)
# Model Overview (for Diagnosis)

The supplied code contains the diagnosis module, not the HSTU implementation. It inspects item embeddings through `view.item_emb` and sequence features through `view.log2feats(sequence)`. The actual trained network is `view.model`; its `itemnum` bounds the item embedding slice.

The probe scores features at every valid training position. It does not explicitly extract a final user representation. The backbone’s feature computation and final-position readout cannot be verified from this code; left-padded histories require the final nonpadding position.

# Diagnosis Inputs & Hooks

`DiagnosisProbe(view, device)` receives the compatibility wrapper and stores its `meta_data`, `review_data`, and `user_train`. Only metadata is subsequently used directly.

The loader supplies `(None, sequence, positive, negative)` with tensors shaped `B × L`. Sequences pass through `log2feats`; positive and negative IDs are stacked into `B × L × 2` and scored using `predict_score(features, items)`. Positions with positive ID zero are excluded. Scoring runs in evaluation mode without gradients.

# Probes & Metrics

- **Embedding collapse:** Samples up to 2,048 real-item embeddings using seed 42, excluding padding and reserved tokens. It normalizes vectors, averages off-diagonal cosine similarities, and maps the result to `[0,1]`. Higher values suggest directional collapse; orthogonal embeddings yield approximately 0.5.
- **Positive–negative separation:** Processes up to ten batches and computes positive minus negative logits. Higher mean and 10th-percentile margins indicate stronger separation. Lower negative-wins and small-margin rates are preferable; the small-margin threshold is 0.5.
- **Category breakdown:** Counts category occurrences separately for positive and negative items in low-margin and wrong-ranking cases, retaining the top 20 categories.

# Perturbation & Tests

No sequence perturbation, shuffling, ablation, or sensitivity test is implemented. Random embedding sampling only limits computational cost.

# MODEL_DIAGNOSIS Schema & Limitations

`run_full_diagnosis` returns `metrics` and `metric_definitions`, covering collapse, four margin statistics, and nested category counts. `diagnosis_interpreter_prompt` embeds these into a prompt requesting status, core findings, implications, and supporting evidence; it does not itself generate that interpretation.

These are training-sample diagnostics, not validation HR@10. Margins depend on score scale and sampled negatives. Available task metadata excludes item categories, so category counts will be empty. Reviews and stored histories are unused. Empty margin samples produce zeros, potentially obscuring missing evidence. The probes do not assess temporal sensitivity, generalization, recommendation coverage, or gradient health.

Substitution alone also cannot establish redundancy for a particular user; histories provide context, but do not prove ownership, fulfilled needs, or intent.

For attribute extraction, [WDC-PAVE (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02130) evaluates extraction and normalization from product titles/descriptions using manually verified labels, including unit conversion and name normalization. This supports extracting explicit connector, format, dimension, and quantity values with supporting text spans. [CatalogRAG (2025)](https://www.amazon.science/publications/catalograg-retrieval-guided-llm-prediction-for-multilingual-e-commerce-product-attributes) instead predicts missing attributes from related catalog entries; such predictions should not be treated as explicit evidence in this audit.

[Selective prediction research (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15610) emphasizes the tradeoff between coverage and error among asserted predictions; its experiments concern vision-language reasoning, so recommendation applicability remains a hypothesis.             HSTU adds learned relative-position and bucketed time biases before SiLU attention aggregation. Meta’s reference implementation uses next-position timestamps, approximately t[i+1]−t[j], with special endpoint handling—not simply t[i]−t[j]. Consequently, deleting and repacking events changes positional distances and can change temporal query anchors even when retained timestamps remain unchanged. Uniformly translating retained positions preserves relative distances; interior deletion generally does not. Audit the supplied implementation’s actual timestamp path, absolute embeddings, masks and normalization before attributing effects to temporal sensitivity. For left padding, read the final nonpadding index, never count−1. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.17152v3), [reference implementation](https://github.com/meta-recsys/generative-recommenders/blob/main/generative_recommenders/research/modeling/sequential/hstu.py).

Suggested controls, inferred from these mechanisms: use identical retained-event subsets in two conditions—fully mask deleted slots while preserving original positions and temporal anchors, versus compact and left-pad normally. Hold tensor length, attention scaling, candidates and readout rules fixed; optionally compact while gathering original bias submatrices to isolate coordinate effects. Compare equal-count oldest, recent and random deletions with the final event fixed; separately remove the final event versus the penultimate event. These contrasts distinguish information loss, recency and repacking effects, although internal holes themselves introduce distribution shift.

For ordering, shuffle only the prefix, preserving the final item, length, item multiset and padding. Compare item-only permutations on fixed chronological timestamp slots against joint item–timestamp permutations; the latter can create nonchronological, out-of-distribution inputs. Include local/block shuffles and final-suffix-preserving variants, identity controls, and repeated permutations with paired uncertainty. Report per-category and macro validation HR@10 changes. Treat degradation as perturbation sensitivity, not proof of temporal reasoning; the paper’s training-time stochastic subsequence selection does not establish robustness to arbitrary inference-time deletion or shuffling.

---

No study located directly validates inference-time deletion/shuffling sensitivity as a predictor of gains from subsequent model changes. Related evidence supports narrower conclusions: [Woolridge et al. (2021)](https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-2955/paper8.pdf) found SASRec relatively robust to history shuffling and highlighted ambiguous timestamps; this tests dependence on ordering, not whether increasing sensitivity improves generalization. [Petrov et al. (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19833) found recency-weighted pairwise models competitive with Transformers across several benchmarks, showing that useful history information need not require higher-order interactions. Neither establishes a diagnostic-to-improvement relationship or transfers directly to HSTU on these four categories.

Methodological inference: training positive–negative margin changes measure sensitivity on observed training targets and sampled competitors; memorization and score-scale changes can inflate them without improving ranks. Paired held-out target-rank changes, keeping each user’s target and candidate set fixed across perturbations, more directly measure ranking dependence. Still, degradation after deletion/shuffling shows reliance under corrupted inputs, not that retraining with a proposed change will help. Deletion also changes history length/recency; shuffling can create out-of-distribution histories. [Krichene and Rendle (2020)](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) demonstrate that sampled ranking metrics can reverse model comparisons; fixed 99-negative candidates support the pinned benchmark comparison, not full-catalog conclusions.

Repeated histories, overlapping prefixes, and multiple perturbations of one user are dependent observations: aggregate paired effects per user and bootstrap users. Repeatedly choosing changes from diagnostic and validation feedback risks adaptive overfitting, as illustrated by [Dwork et al. (2015)](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper/2015/hash/bad5f33780c42f2588878a9d07405083-Abstract.html). Treat sensitivity as hypothesis generation, with no defensible numerical uplift forecast; prioritize controlled, single-model HSTU ablations of loss, sampling, regularization, and recency treatment, selected by the fixed macro validation HR@10.
